# Slide 1


### Notes
The great dragon danced and spun and trod the air over the city. Its colour was moonlight, gleaming off its scales. Sometimes it would twist and glide with deceptive speed over the rooftops for the sheer joy of existing.
And it was all wrong, Vimes thought. Part of him was marvelling at the sheer beauty of the sight, but an insistent, weaselly little group of brain cells from the wrong side of the synapses was scrawling its graffiti on the walls of wonderment.
It's a bloody great lizard, they jeered. Must weigh tons. Nothing that big can fly, not even on beautiful wings. And what is a flying lizard doing with great big scales on its back?
Five hundred feet above him a lance of blue-white flame roared into the sky.
It can't do something like that! It'd burn its own lips off!
[...]
He was trying to remember its shape. As in the case with many things that are totally familiar, he hadn't really looked at it for years. Now he was trying to convince himself that the forest of little turrets and crenellations at its top looked just the same tonight as they had done yesterday.
It was giving him some difficulty.
Without taking his eyes off it, he grabbed Sgt Colon's shoulder and gently pointed him in the right direction.
He said, "Can you see anything odd about the top of the tower?"
Colon stared up for a while, and then laughed nervously. "Well, it looks like there's a dragon sitting on it, doesn't it?"
"Yes. That's what I thought."
"Only, only, only when you sort of look properly, you can see it's just made up out of shadows and clumps of ivy and that. I mean, if you half-close one eye, it looks like two old women and a wheelbarrow."
Vimes tried this. "Nope," he said. "It still looks like a dragon. A huge one. Sort of hunched up, and looking down. Look, you can see its wings folded up."
"Beg pardon, sir. That's just a broken turret giving the effect."
[...]
Then Vimes said, "Tell me, Sergeant — I ask in a spirit of pure inquiry — what do you think's causing the effect of a pair of huge wings unfurling?"
Colon swallowed.
"I think that's caused by a pair of huge wings, sir," he said.
"Spot on, Sergeant."

# Slide 5: @chrissbaumann.bsky.social

@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD

### Notes
Context

In Hogfather, the Auditors of Reality have arranged for the assassination of the Hogfather — the Discworld’s version of Santa Claus — as part of their quest to remove irrationality from the universe. When belief in the Hogfather starts to fade, the sun itself is threatened, for on the Disc, belief quite literally sustains reality.
Susan, Death’s granddaughter, becomes aware that something is terribly wrong: the Hogfather has been “removed,” and with him the world’s collective belief in wonder and kindness. Everyone else, however, seems paralyzed — waiting for someone else to do something. 

Quote

The Hogfather had been—well, not exactly kidnapped. More... removed.

Someone had to do something. It was like that time when Twyla’s grandmother had started telling everyone that she was the Empress of Krull and had stopped wearing clothes.

And Susan was bright enough to know that the phrase “Someone ought to do something” was not, by itself, a helpful one. People who used it never added the rider “and that someone is me.”

But someone ought to do something, and right now the whole pool of someones consisted of her, and no one else.

She stared at the fireplace, where the Hogfather’s image shimmered faintly in the fading glow. The world was teetering on the edge of unreality, and still no one was doing anything — because no one thought it was their job.

All right, she thought grimly, if the universe wants to play silly games, I’ll play too. Someone has to keep things running.

She picked up the poker and straightened her back. “Fine,” she said aloud. “Let’s get this sorted out.”

# Slide 6: Pluralistic Ignorance - What?

- Collective inaction
- Institutionalised denial
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
The quote from Discworld is an example of pluralistic ignorance - but what is that? It can be expressed as for instance; 
Collective inaction where
Everyone senses the danger, but each assumes that someone else, someone more qualified, better positioned — will act. 
Self-perpetuating paralysis: The belief that “someone should do something” satisfies moral urgency while excusing personal responsibility.
Everyone assumes maintaining appearances is better than confronting the truth, leaving real problems unaddressed
or Institutionalized denial, where a bureaucracy sustains order through illusion rather than substance.

---

# Slide 7: Pluralistic Ignorance - Examples

- Risky last minute change not raised
- No ticket created, release ships
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
Real life examples of this could be; 
A large Go/No-Go meeting where several engineers notice a risky last-minute configuration change; no one speaks because the room is quiet and the status board shows “green.” 
A security review: Multiple reviewers sees a high-severity issue, assuming “someone else will file the blocker,” and move on. No ticket is created and the release ships with the potential risk

---

# Slide 8: Pluralistic Ignorance - Consequences

- Larger groups  →  effect gets worse
- Norm drift & alienation
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
What are the consequences of this?

Lower intervention rates and slower responses, and this is getting worse as group size grows

Norm drift & alienation: People conform away from private beliefs when they misread peers’ attitudes
meaning that you might change your beliefs based on what you ma  incorrectly consider to be the norm.

---

# Slide 9: Pluralistic Ignorance - Why?

- Norms
- Inherent fear of being the odd one out
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
Why is that?

Norms govern appropriate behavior in certain contexts,
such as in the classroom, at a party, in a boardroom, or in a hospital, 
as well as social behavior with certain people, 
such as friends, strangers, or colleagues.

These norms dictate, for example, that one should show public support for friends and colleagues, 
should not challenge others” personal choices, 
and should appear calm, collected, and in control at all times.

---

# Slide 10: Pluralistic Ignorance - Solution

- Psychological safety
- Make ownership explicit
- Norm-correction messaging
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
How to solve this?

- Create psychological safety & voice: eg by leaders invite & thank for dissent
- Make ownership explicit, eg by assigning a decision owner
- Periodically publish “what we actually do here”, shown to counter pluralistic ignorance

In a world full of bystanders, the only one who acts is the person who realizes there is no “someone else.”

# Slide 11: @chrissbaumann.bsky.social

@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD

### Notes
Context

After uncovering a political conspiracy, surviving assassination attempts, and nearly watching the city fall apart, William de Worde and his newspaper crew at The Ankh-Morpork Times find themselves back at the presses. The chaos has passed, and everyone seems eager to pretend that nothing unusual happened — to get “back to normal.” But as William reflects, the public has already absorbed the whole extraordinary ordeal as just another day in Ankh-Morpork. 

Quote

“‘Yes, no more of this stuff, Otto,’ he said.

‘Damn right,’ said Goodmountain.

‘Let’s just try to get back to normal and get a paper out, shall we?’

‘You mean normal where mad priests start to collect dogs, or normal where vampires mess around with evil shadows?’ said Gowdie.

‘I mean like normal before that,’ said William.

‘Oh, I see. You mean like back in the old days,’ said Gowdie.

‘Yes,’ said William firmly. ‘Before all this started.’

‘That would be about three months ago,’ said Goodmountain. ‘When you came along and started all this, Mr. de Worde.’

William hesitated. ‘Yes,’ he said, ‘well... let’s just call it a return to normal anyway.’

[...]

Later, as the presses rumbled and the smell of hot ink filled the air, William stood watching the first copies of the Times roll out.

He’d expected that to... what? Inform people? Yes. Annoy people? Well, some people, at least. What he hadn’t expected was that it wouldn’t make any difference.

The paper came out, and it didn’t matter. The world went on.

The great events of the past days — the murders, the lies, the revelations — were already turning into yesterday’s stories.

People just seemed to accept things.

Ankh-Morpork went on being Ankh-Morpork.”

# Slide 12: Normalcy bias - what?

- Normalization of disruption
- Denial of change
- Collective reassurance
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
So everything was back to normal, but, what is even normal, or how do we perceive “normal”?
Normalization of disruption: Even after major upheaval, the characters and the city instantly revert to “normal” routines.
Denial of change: People reshape shocking events to fit their prior mental model — “this is just how things are.”
Normalcy bias made literal: “People just seemed to accept things” captures how societies instinctively downplay issues  

---

# Slide 13: Normalcy bias - Examples

- Team ships despite new data
- Covid-19
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
Examples of normalcy bias could be; 
Release readiness: For quarters the pipeline is “green,” so the team ships despite new metrics shows a different picture, assuming all the red flags is just noise - because, prod environment is usually fine
Covid-19: In the early days of the pandemic, although the authorities urged people to practice social distancing, many people continued living their lives as usual: media footage showed crowded bars and beaches and indicated that many people were acting like there was no crisis.
The fact that this was an invisible threat made things worse: many people didn’t know anyone with an infection or hadn’t seen anyone seriously ill. Due to this, they thought COVID wasn’t much of a threat and it wouldn’t affect them personally. They “normalized” an unusual situation and carried on with their everyday routines, even when urged to take precautions. This was normalcy bias at work.

---

# Slide 14: @chrissbaumann.bsky.social

Normalcy bias - Consequences
- Delayed action in emerging crises
- Failure to adapt  to changing circumstances
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD

### Notes
Potential consequences are that
- warnings are discounted and time-to-response increases. 
- but also failure to adapt to changing circumstances

---

# Slide 15: Normalcy bias - Why?

- Schema/expectation lock-in
- Ambiguity & social proof
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
Two main reasons for that to happen- 
- we fit signals into existing models (“this is fine”) to reduce cognitive load; it’s a “system 1 VS 2” issue; 
Our brain consists of 2 systems; System 1 is fast & intuitive. System 2 is slower, deliberate, and logical.
System 1 handles automatic tasks like detecting distance or reacting to a sudden stimulus. 
System 2 is used for more complex tasks that require conscious effort, like solving a difficult math problem. 
The issue here is that that evolutionary should use system 1 most of the the time, 
but in modern life we tend to use system 2 too much, which can lead to fatigue and also will impact system 1, 
and eventually lead to poor judgements such as instance normalcy.

- Also: under unclear threat, people seek confirmation, which delays action and preserves yesterday’s normal

---

# Slide 16: Normalcy bias - Solution

- Hard rules & guardrails
- Risk analysis & scenario drills
- Decision ownership
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
How to solve this:
- Define objective triggers, eg SLO breaches, or “status changes to orange”, that require an action. Do not go for subjective “measurements” like “it seems fine”.
- Analyse potential risks upfront, and rehearse “what if the trend continues or accelerates?” to widen the expectation set and reduce default-to-normal
- Name a person who is in charge of handling certain decisions and has the authority to execute and/or halt; this removes diffusion and speeds deviation from “normal.”

---

# Slide 17: @chrissbaumann.bsky.social

@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD

### Notes
Context

Lord Vetinari, the coldly rational ruler of Ankh-Morpork, takes a famously bureaucratic approach to chaos. Instead of fighting crime, he legalizes it — converting theft into a regulated civic service. The newly recognized Thieves’ Guild operates on quotas and annual plans: a fixed number of thefts per year, fairly distributed, receipts issued, and “unauthorized crime” punished. The city’s problem is no longer crime itself, but deviation from target. 

Quote

“One of the Patrician’s greatest contributions to the reliable operation of Ankh-Morpork had been, very early in his administration, the legalising of the ancient Guild of Thieves. Crime was always with us, he reasoned, and therefore, if you were going to have crime, it at least should be organised crime.

And so the Guild had been encouraged to come out of the shadows and build a big Guildhouse, take their place at civic banquets, and set up their training college with day-release courses and City and Guilds certificates and everything. In exchange for the winding down of the Watch, they agreed, while trying to keep their faces straight, to keep crime levels to a level to be determined annually. That way, everyone could plan ahead, said Lord Vetinari, and part of the uncertainty had been removed from the chaos that is life.

And then, a little while later, the Patrician summoned the leading thieves again and said, oh, by the way, there was something else. What was it, now? Oh, yes...

I know who you are, he said. I know where you live. I know what kind of horse you ride. I know where your wife has her hair done. I know where your lovely children, how old are they now, my, doesn’t time fly, I know where they play. So you won’t forget about what we agreed, will you? And he smiled.

So did they, after a fashion.

And in fact it had turned out very satisfactorily from everyone’s point of view. [...]

A complicated arrangement of receipts and vouchers saw to it that, while everyone was eligible for the attentions of the Guild, no-one had too much, and this was very acceptable—at least to those citizens who were rich enough to afford the quite reasonable premiums the Guild charged for an uninterrupted life. There was a strange foreign word for this: inn-sewer-ants.

No-one knew exactly what it had originally meant, but Ankh-Morpork had made it its own.”

Footnote 6: “One of the remarkable innovations introduced by the Patrician was to make the Thieves’ Guild responsible for theft, with annual budgets, forward planning and, above all, rigid job protection. Thus, in return for an agreed average level of crime per annum, the thieves themselves saw to it that unauthorised crime was met with the full force of Injustice, which was generally a stick with nails in it.”

# Slide 18: Metric fixation - What?

- Metric fixation as governance
- Goodhart’s Law in action
- Perverse incentives
- Illusion of control through numbers
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
Guess everyone has experienced this before
Metric fixation as governance: In this example crime is no longer prevented — it’s managed against a numerical target.
Goodhart’s Law in action: Charles Goodhart is a British economist, famous for the saying; "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure". Here in the quote the goal “reduce crime” becomes the metric “stay within the yearly quota”, and hence, corrupting the intent.
Perverse incentives: Success is defined by meeting crime quotas, not by improving public safety.
Illusion of control through numbers: Vetinari replaces moral order with measurable order — the city looks “efficient,” even though nothing has truly improved.

---

# Slide 19: Metric fixation - Examples

- X % test coverage as target
- Velocity / story points as performance metric
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
Examples from our world could be
Having X % test coverage as target: Teams are rewarded for coverage %, so they add meaningless tests 
Velocity / story points as performance metric: Leadership uses “velocity” to judge team productivity, or compare teams against each other 

---

# Slide 20: Metric fixation - Consequences

- The metric gets gamed, the system is distorted
- Trust decays
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
Consequences are that
- metric gets gamed and the system is distorted. one classic pattern is teachers that just “teach to the test”
- also trust decays, Eg stakeholders start managing to fake “green dashboards,” but not the real quality, which hides real risk until something explodes. 

---

# Slide 21: Metric fixation - Why?

- We want certainty
- Incentives shape behavior
- Surrogation
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
Why this is happening?
- Because we want certainty: Numbers feel objective, controllable, comparable. In complex work, leaders grab a simple metric to reduce ambiguity and create the illusion of control.
- Incentives shape behavior, meaning: Once rewards, praise, or pressure are tied to a number, people rationally adapt behavior to hit that number with the least pain — even if that breaks the purpose.
- Also people start believing “the metric is the goal.” High velocity is mistaken for “delivering value”. High coverage means quality. The proxy replaces the thing it was meant to approximate.

---

# Slide 22: Metric fixation - Solution

- State the actual goal
- Multi dimensional metrics
- Look at qualitative signals
- Use metrics for their intent
- Evaluate metrics regularly
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
Let’s look at some potential solutions:
- State the actual goal (e.g. “fewer production defects that hurt users”) 
and review regularly whether the metric still tracks that goal. Kill or adjust metrics that drift. 
- Instead of one hero number, deliver multiple combined metrics, eg delivery metric + quality metric + sustainability metric 
(e.g. “Throughput AND escaped defects AND on-call load”). If one spikes, that’s a red flag. This makes gaming harder.
Also looking at qualitative signals, using metrics for their intent and regular evaluation of metrics in place help.

---

Commander Sam Vimes faces escalating chaos in Ankh-Morpork: dwarfs and trolls on the brink of war, the Watch stretched thin, and political pressure from above.

‘You wanted me, sir?’ he said, turning to Vetinari again. ‘There’s a Silicon Anti-Defamation League march in Water Street, and I’ve got traffic backed up all the way to Least Gate—’

‘Well, at any rate I’m sure your men can deal with it,’ said Vetinari.”

# Slide 24: Pesticide Paradox - What?

- False reassurance through routine
- Institutional self satisfaction
- Signal erosion
- Satirical bureaucracy
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
Pesticide Paradox refers to the fact that when you use a pesticide on a certain lifeform for to long, that lifeform becomes immune to the pesticide. In this quote it’s expressed as
False reassurance through routine: Vetinari treats novel civic chaos as ordinary — “the Watch can handle it.”
Institutional self satisfaction: The city relies on the same old “controls” (bureaucracy, patrols) without re-examining their adequacy.
Signal erosion: Real escalation (racial violence, civic unrest) gets reframed as normal “progress.”
Satirical bureaucracy: Vetinari’s calm denial parodies how systems optimize for the appearance of stability rather than adaptive change.

---

# Slide 25: Pesticide Paradox - Examples

- A stale end-to-end regression pack
- Low-value unit tests
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
A couple of perhaps not unfamiliar examples;
A stale end-to-end regression pack. The team has 500 automated UI tests. They’ve run every night for a year. All pass. Product owners use that dashboard to claim “quality is good.” Reality: major new flows aren’t covered, so those defects slip to prod. The suite is now testing yesterday’s system, not today’s, which is a textbook pesticide paradox: unchanged tests stop surfacing new faults in an evolving system.
Low-value unit tests written only to pass coverage gates. (Devs wrote trivial “assert not-null/no-throw” tests to push coverage to 85%. Coverage stays high, leadership is happy, and nobody feels pressure to add stronger assertions later. After multiple refactors, logic bugs in boundary cases sneak through because the high-coverage tests don’t actually check behavior anymore. The metric is still green; the defects evolved around it)

---

# Slide 26: Pesticide Paradox - Consequences

- False confidence / silent drift
- Quality blindness becomes institutional
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
Consequences are
- False confidence or silent drift: as just described in the examples
- Also metrics become compliance theater (“All’s well!”), 
so leadership underfunds exploratory testing, maintenance of tests, or refactoring 
and risk accumulates quietly.

---

# Slide 27: Pesticide Paradox - Why?

- Habituation & routine trust
- Sunk cost & inertia
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
This happens because of
- habituation + routine trust, because Humans generalize from past success: 
“These tests caught bugs before, so if they’re green now, we’re fine.” 
Our brains overweight familiar signals and underweight novel threats. 
- Also, teams that invested months building and maintaining a test suite rarely admit the suite is losing effectiveness, 
since it would feel like admitting wasted effort, 
so they keep re-running it unchanged instead of questioning it

---

# Slide 28: Pesticide Paradox - Solution

- Deliberate variation  → new “pesticides”
- For our testing examples
  - Continuously evolve tests
  - Exploratory testing
  - “What changed?” review
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
As a general solution, use deliberate variation aka new “pesticides”.

For our testing examples, this for example could be:
Continuously evolve tests with the product, 
Exploratory Testing as a first-class activity and “What changed?” reviews

- Ask open questions
- There are no stupid questions
- Be open minded
- Do active listening
- Know your peers
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
Ask open questions and ask frequently!
The term “There are no stupid questions” is true
Be open minded / open your mind
Do active listening
Know your peers, stakeholders, documentation and where to find it, domain, etc.…

# Slide 31: Notice problems without actively looking for them

- Cultivate psychological safety
- Set objective triggers
- Assign explicit ownership
- Tune into qualitative noise
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
- Cultivate psychological safety: It cannot be said often enough, psychological safety is super important, and leaders must explicitly invite dissent and thank those who raise blockers to break the silence
- Set objective triggers: Establish hard rules and guardrails that force action based on data, removing the option for subjective "it seems fine" assessments .
- Assign explicit ownership: Designate specific decision owners or incident commanders to eliminate the "someone else will do it" diffusion of responsibility.
- Tune into qualitative noise: Monitor human signals—user narratives, retro notes, and pain reports—to detect systemic distortions that quantitative charts often hide.

# Slide 32: Wrap up

- Problems aren’t  immediately recognized
- Methods to improve  your problem recognizing skills
- Applying & practicing techniques
@tg2g.bsky.social
\#agileTD
@chrissbaumann.bsky.social

### Notes
To wrap up:

- Some problems aren’t immediately recognized, 
sometimes our brain makes us not see the dragon that’s attacking our city.
- But there are methods to improve your problem recognizing skills, 
such as cultivating psychological safety and setting objective triggers.
- Applying & practicing techniques like asking open questions and active listening 
can help you to recognise problems without actively having to think about them.
